There is a particular kind of silence that belongs only to early morning, before the city remembers its own noise. The streets seem washed in blue light, and even the air feels unopened, like a letter no one has yet read. In that hour, small things become vivid: the click of a kettle, the shape of steam rising from a cup, the way a curtain moves without wind.

I have always loved these beginnings. They offer a strange permission to be unfinished. The day has not yet demanded decisions, achievements, or explanations. It simply waits, patient and blank, while the mind gathers itself. Sometimes I think we are most honest in such moments, before we put on our public faces and rehearse the scripts of work, friendship, and obligation.

There is comfort, too, in routine. The same coffee, the same window, the same few minutes of stillness can become a private ritual, a way of saying, I am here. Habits are often dismissed as dull, but they can also be anchors. They hold us steady when the world feels too fast or too loud.

Maybe that is why mornings matter: they remind us that life is not only made of great events. It is stitched together from quiet repetitions, from ordinary things noticed carefully. And if we pay attention, even a simple beginning can feel like a small, daily grace. In those fleeting minutes, we remember ourselves not as roles, but as breathing, wondering, imperfect, unfinished, hopeful people once more.
